content.title: About
content.content: Khorasan (also known as farro, emmer, or “ancient wheat”) is a large grain derived from the ancient wheat species Triticum turgidum ssp. turanicum. It has a nutty, slightly sweet flavor and a firm, slightly crunchy texture. Khorasan can be eaten raw after soaking, as well as boiled, baked, or used in breads and pastries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Khorasan is considered one of the oldest cultivated wheat varieties, grown more than 7,000 years ago in the Near East.
The grain is larger than modern wheat and has a deep golden‑brown color.
Compared with most modern wheat, Khorasan contains higher levels of protein and minerals.
It is often called a “future food” because of its nutritional profile and drought‑resistance.
In several cultures Khorasan is used in traditional dishes such as couscous, salads, and soups.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Khorasan provides about 15 % protein, higher than most common wheat varieties, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, phosphorus, zinc, and iron, essential for bones, nerves, and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in Khorasan help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with regular wheat, Khorasan raises blood glucose more slowly, beneficial for weight management and diabetes.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease may react to Khorasan and should avoid it.

items.title: Contains gluten
items.content: Khorasan is not suitable for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Phosphorus excess
items.content: Very large portions can lead to excess phosphorus intake, which may be problematic for kidney disease patients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak Khorasan for 8–12 hours, then boil until tender (about 30–40 minutes). Use it in salads, soups, grain‑based puddings, as a side dish, or add it to bread and pastry dough. Dried grains can be toasted and added to granola.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Khorasan in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer. Discard any grains that develop a moldy or rancid smell.
